pos: n. (the side of the face; rendering Hebrew lechi, Greek siagon)
etymology: Old English ceace. The cheek is where an insult lands rather than a wound — a blow there is contempt before it is injury.
biblical_def: The cheek is the side of the face. Christ commands, “whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also” (Mat 5:39). Lamentations counsels the same: “He giveth his cheek to him that smiteth him: he is filled full with reproach” (Lam 3:30). Isaiah's Servant says, “I gave my back to the smiters, and my cheeks to them that plucked off the hair” (Isa 50:6), and Micah foretells that they shall smite the judge of Israel “with a rod upon the cheek” (Mic 5:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines cheek as the side of the face below the eyes on each side; and among mechanics, the sides of many things, as of a press.
webster_full: CHEEK, n. The side of the face below the eyes on each side.
2. Among mechanics, cheeks are those pieces of a machine which form corresponding sides, or which are double and alike.
scriptures: Mat 5:39
But I say unto you, That ye resist not evil: but whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also.
Lam 3:30
He giveth his cheek to him that smiteth him: he is filled full with reproach.
Isa 50:6
I gave my back to the smiters, and my cheeks to them that plucked off the hair: I hid not my face from shame and spitting.
Mic 5:1
Now gather thyself in troops, O daughter of troops: he hath laid siege against us: they shall smite the judge of Israel with a rod upon the cheek.
corruption_summary: Turning the cheek is read as passivity toward violence, and the blow in view is an insult — a backhand to the right cheek, which was a legal humiliation rather than an assault.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew 5:39 specifies the right cheek, and the detail carries the meaning. A right-handed man striking another's right cheek must use the back of his hand, which in that culture was a formal insult delivered to an inferior, not a fight. Turning the other cheek offers the left — which can only be struck with an open palm, the blow given between equals. The response is not submission to violence but a refusal to accept the terms of the humiliation.

Isaiah 50:6 is the Servant doing it before it was taught: I gave my back to the smiters, and my cheeks to them that plucked off the hair: I hid not my face from shame and spitting. The next verse gives the ground — for the Lord GOD will help me; therefore shall I not be confounded. Absorbing an insult is only bearable for someone certain of vindication from elsewhere.
roots_summary: Hebrew lechi (H3895), cheek or jaw — also the jawbone Samson used; Greek siagon (G4600), the cheek or jawbone.
roots_lines: Hebrew lechi (H3895) — cheek, jaw; Lamentations 3:30, Micah 5:1, Judges 15:15.
Greek siagon (G4600) — cheek; Matthew 5:39, Luke 6:29.
Greek rhapizo (G4474) — to strike with the back of the hand; Matthew 5:39.
usage: “Smite thee on thy right cheek” — a backhand, and therefore an insult.
“He giveth his cheek to him that smiteth him” — Lamentations counselling the same.
“I hid not my face from shame and spitting” — the Servant, before it was taught.

pos: adj. (glad, of good spirit; rendering Hebrew tob, Greek hilaros)
etymology: From cheer, originally the face or countenance — cheerfulness is what shows on the face before it is a mood.
biblical_def: Cheerful means glad. Paul names it as the manner God loves in giving: “God loveth a cheerful giver” (2Co 9:7), and lists it among the gifts — “he that sheweth mercy, with cheerfulness” (Rom 12:8). Proverbs makes it physical: “A merry heart doeth good like a medicine: but a broken spirit drieth the bones” (Pro 17:22), and “a merry heart maketh a cheerful countenance” (Pro 15:13). Zechariah tells Israel's fasts shall become cheerful feasts (Zec 8:19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines cheerful as lively; animated; having good spirits; and full of life; gay; and expressive of good spirits or joy.
webster_full: CHEERFUL, a. Lively; animated; having good spirits; moderately joyful.
2. Full of life; gay; animated; mirthful; musical.
3. Expressive of good spirits or joy; as a cheerful countenance.
scriptures: Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.
Rom 12:8
Or he that exhorteth, on exhortation: he that giveth, let him do it with simplicity; he that ruleth, with diligence; he that sheweth mercy, with cheerfulness.
A merry heart doeth good like a medicine: but a broken spirit drieth the bones.
A merry heart maketh a cheerful countenance: but by sorrow of the heart the spirit is broken.
corruption_summary: Duty is thought to excuse a grim manner, and Scripture repeatedly attaches the manner to the command — give cheerfully, show mercy with cheerfulness.
corruption_paragraphs: 2 Corinthians 9:7 does not merely require giving; it specifies the disposition: every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver. The Greek hilaros gives us hilarious. God's stated preference is not for the largest gift but for the gladdest, which means a reluctant large gift and a joyful small one are not ranked the way a treasurer would rank them.

Romans 12:8 applies the same principle to mercy: he that sheweth mercy, with cheerfulness. Mercy delivered with a sigh has been half-withdrawn in the giving. Anyone who has received grudging help knows the manner is part of the gift, and Paul treats the manner as belonging to the gift itself rather than as an optional garnish on it.
roots_summary: Greek hilaros (G2431), cheerful, merry — the root of hilarious; hilarotes (G2432), cheerfulness; Hebrew tob leb, good of heart.
roots_lines: Greek hilaros (G2431) — cheerful; only 2 Corinthians 9:7.
Greek hilarotes (G2432) — cheerfulness; only Romans 12:8.
Hebrew leb sameach — merry heart; Proverbs 15:13, 17:22.
usage: “God loveth a cheerful giver” — the manner ranked above the amount.
“He that sheweth mercy, with cheerfulness” — the manner belongs to the gift.
“A merry heart doeth good like a medicine” — cheerfulness as physiology.

pos: n. (an order of angelic being; rendering Hebrew kerub)
etymology: A transliteration of Hebrew kerub, of uncertain root. Scripture's cherubim are guardians of holiness, not the infants of later art.
biblical_def: A cherub is an angelic guardian. Cherubims with a flaming sword keep the way of the tree of life after the fall (Gen 3:24). Two of gold face each other over the mercy seat, and God says, “there I will meet with thee, and I will commune with thee from above the mercy seat, from between the two cherubims” (Exo 25:22). David sings that God “rode upon a cherub, and did fly” (Psa 18:10), and Ezekiel addresses the king of Tyrus as “the anointed cherub that covereth” (Eze 28:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines cherub as a figure composed of various creatures, as a man, an ox, an eagle or lion; and an order of angels, of which the plural is cherubim or cherubs.
webster_full: CHERUB, n. plu. CHERUBS or CHERUBIM. A figure composed of various creatures, as a man, an ox, an eagle or lion.
2. A celestial spirit; an angel of the second order.
scriptures: Gen 3:24
So he drove out the man; and he placed at the east of the garden of Eden Cherubims, and a flaming sword which turned every way, to keep the way of the tree of life.

And there I will meet with thee, and I will commune with thee from above the mercy seat, from between the two cherubims which are upon the ark of the testimony, of all things which I will give thee in commandment unto the children of Israel.
And he rode upon a cherub, and did fly: yea, he did fly upon the wings of the wind.
Thou art the anointed cherub that covereth; and I have set thee so: thou wast upon the holy mountain of God; thou hast walked up and down in the midst of the stones of fire.
corruption_summary: Cherubim have been reduced to decorative infants, and Scripture stations them with a flaming sword at the gate of Eden and over the place of atonement.
corruption_paragraphs: The two appearances belong together. In Genesis 3:24 cherubim and a flaming sword guard the way to the tree of life — the entrance is closed and defended. In Exodus 25:22 two cherubim of beaten gold stand over the mercy seat, facing each other and looking down at the blood-sprinkled lid, and God says there I will meet with thee. The same beings that barred the way at Eden now flank the place where God meets sinners. The route back is through atonement.

Ezekiel 28:14 places a cherub in the highest possible position — thou art the anointed cherub that covereth; and I have set thee so — and then records the fall: thine heart was lifted up because of thy beauty. Whatever the passage's primary reference to Tyre, the church has long read a warning in it about the highest created excellence being no protection against pride.
roots_summary: Hebrew kerub (H3742), cherub; plural kerubim; kapporeth (H3727), mercy seat — the lid the cherubim overshadow.
roots_lines: Hebrew kerub (H3742) — cherub; Genesis 3:24, Exodus 25:18-22, Ezekiel 10:1-20.
Hebrew kapporeth (H3727) — mercy seat, covering; Exodus 25:22, the meeting place.
Hebrew sakak (H5526) — to cover, overshadow; Ezekiel 28:14, the cherub that covereth.
usage: “Cherubims, and a flaming sword… to keep the way of the tree of life” — the gate closed.
“From between the two cherubims” — the same guardians over the mercy seat.
“The anointed cherub that covereth” — height that did not prevent a fall.

etymology: From Old French cote. The biblical coat is the inner tunic worn next to the body — and three of them carry a great deal of the Bible's weight.
biblical_def: A coat is a tunic. God makes the first: “unto Adam also and to his wife did the LORD God make coats of skins, and clothed them” (Gen 3:21). Jacob makes Joseph one of many colours, and the brothers strip it off him (Gen 37:3,23). Christ's was “without seam, woven from the top throughout”, and the soldiers cast lots rather than tear it (Joh 19:23–24). Hannah made Samuel a little coat yearly (1Sa 2:19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines coat as an upper garment, of whatever material it may be made; the garment worn by men over the waistcoat; and a petticoat, the garment of a woman or child.
webster_full: COAT, n. An upper garment, of whatever material it may be made.
2. A petticoat; a garment worn by infants or young children.
3. The habit or vesture, as an emblem of the office.
4. That on which ensigns armorial are portrayed; usually called a coat of arms.
scriptures: Gen 3:21
Unto Adam also and to his wife did the LORD God make coats of skins, and clothed them.
Gen 37:3
Now Israel loved Joseph more than all his children, because he was the son of his old age: and he made him a coat of many colours.
Then the soldiers, when they had crucified Jesus, took his garments, and made four parts, to every soldier a part; and also his coat: now the coat was without seam, woven from the top throughout.
Moreover his mother made him a little coat, and brought it to him from year to year, when she came up with her husband to offer the yearly sacrifice.
corruption_summary: Clothing is treated as trivial in Scripture, and three coats carry the fall, a family's fracture, and the seamless garment gambled for at the cross.
corruption_paragraphs: The first coat and the last belong together. In Eden God kills to clothe two people who had sewn fig leaves; at Golgotha soldiers strip a seamless coat off a Man and gamble for it. Between the two, Joseph's coat is torn from him by his brothers and returned to his father dipped in blood. Every one of the three involves someone being covered or uncovered, and the pattern is not accidental in a book that ends with robes washed white.

John notes the seamless coat's construction with unusual care — woven from the top throughout — and records the soldiers' reasoning: let us not rend it, but cast lots for it, whose it shall be. Even the men executing Him preserved that one garment intact. John says it fulfilled a psalm, and the detail has been read for centuries as an image of a righteousness that cannot be divided into portions.
roots_summary: Hebrew kethoneth (H3801), a tunic; kethoneth passim, the coat of many colours or of long sleeves; Greek chiton (G5509), an inner garment.
roots_lines: Hebrew kethoneth (H3801) — coat, tunic; Genesis 3:21, 37:3, 23, 31-33.
Greek chiton (G5509) — coat, tunic; John 19:23, Matthew 5:40, Luke 6:29.
Greek arraphos (G729) — seamless; only John 19:23.
usage: “Coats of skins, and clothed them” — the first covering, at the cost of a death.
“A coat of many colours” — a father's favour and a family's fracture.
“Without seam, woven from the top throughout” — preserved by the men killing Him.

etymology: Old English cocc, imitative. The cock is Scripture's clock, and its crowing marks one of the New Testament's turning points.
biblical_def: A cock is a rooster. Its crowing measured the night: Christ warns His disciples to watch, “for ye know not when the master of the house cometh, at even, or at midnight, or at the cockcrowing, or in the morning” (Mar 13:35). It fixes the hour of Peter's denial in all four Gospels — “before the cock crow, thou shalt deny me thrice” (Mat 26:34) — and John records the moment plainly: “Peter then denied again: and immediately the cock crew” (Joh 18:27).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines cock as the male of birds, particularly of gallinaceous or domestic fowls; and cockcrowing, the time at which cocks crow, early morning.
webster_full: COCK, n. The male of birds, particularly of gallinaceous or domestic fowls.
2. A weathercock.
3. A spout; an instrument to draw out or discharge liquor from a cask.
COCK-CROWING, n. The time at which cocks crow; early morning.
scriptures: Watch ye therefore: for ye know not when the master of the house cometh, at even, or at midnight, or at the cockcrowing, or in the morning:
Jesus said unto him, Verily I say unto thee, That this night, before the cock crow, thou shalt deny me thrice.
Peter then denied again: and immediately the cock crew.
And the Lord turned, and looked upon Peter. And Peter remembered the word of the Lord, how he had said unto him, Before the cock crow, thou shalt deny me thrice.
corruption_summary: Watchfulness is imagined as heightened alertness, and Christ measures it by whether a man is found doing his duty at whatever hour the master returns.
corruption_paragraphs: Mark 13:35 divides the night into four Roman watches and names them: at even, or at midnight, or at the cockcrowing, or in the morning. The command attached is watch. What Christ describes is not vigilance in the sense of staring at the horizon but a servant found at his post whenever the door opens. The cockcrowing is simply one of the hours — and it is the hour at which Peter, told to watch in Gethsemane, discovered what his sleeping had cost.

Luke 22:61 supplies the detail that makes the crowing bearable: and the Lord turned, and looked upon Peter. And Peter remembered the word of the Lord. The bird was not the instrument of the rebuke; the look was. A rooster's ordinary noise at dawn coincided with a glance across a courtyard, and a man's restoration began.
roots_summary: Greek alektor (G220), a cock; alektorophonia (G219), cockcrowing — the third watch of the night, roughly midnight to three.
roots_lines: Greek alektor (G220) — cock; Matthew 26:34, 74-75, John 18:27, Mark 14:30.
Greek alektorophonia (G219) — cockcrowing, a night watch; only Mark 13:35.
Greek gregoreo (G1127) — to watch; Mark 13:35-37, the command attached.
usage: “At even, or at midnight, or at the cockcrowing, or in the morning” — four watches, one command.
“Before the cock crow, thou shalt deny me thrice” — recorded in all four Gospels.
“Immediately the cock crew” — and the Lord turned and looked.

pos: n., adj. (absence of heat; also of love; rendering Hebrew qar, Greek psuchros)
etymology: Old English cald. Scripture moves the word from weather to affection, and Christ's use of it is the more alarming.
biblical_def: Cold is the absence of heat. Christ names it as a sign: “because iniquity shall abound, the love of many shall wax cold” (Mat 24:12). He offers a cup of cold water as the smallest measurable kindness with a reward attached (Mat 10:42). Revelation's word to Laodicea uses it structurally: “I know thy works, that thou art neither cold nor hot: I would thou wert cold or hot” (Rev 3:15). Proverbs says good news from a far country is “as cold waters to a thirsty soul” (Pro 25:25).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines cold as not warm or hot; gelid; frigid; and figuratively, wanting passion, zeal or ardor; indifferent; unconcerned; not animated.
webster_full: COLD, a. Not warm or hot; gelid; frigid.
2. Having the sensation of cold; chill; shivering.
3. Indifferent; unconcerned; not animated, or easily excited into action.
4. Unaffecting; not able to move the passions.
5. Reserved; coy; not affectionate, cordial or friendly.
scriptures: And because iniquity shall abound, the love of many shall wax cold.
And whosoever shall give to drink unto one of these little ones a cup of cold water only in the name of a disciple, verily I say unto you, he shall in no wise lose his reward.
Rev 3:15
I know thy works, that thou art neither cold nor hot: I would thou wert cold or hot.
As cold waters to a thirsty soul, so is good news from a far country.
corruption_summary: Cooling love is attributed to circumstance or personality, and Christ names one cause — because iniquity shall abound, the love of many shall wax cold.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew 24:12 states a mechanism rather than a mood: because iniquity shall abound, the love of many shall wax cold. Sustained exposure to widespread wrongdoing chills affection. That is worth knowing because the cooling feels like realism from the inside — a person who has been lied to often enough stops trusting, and calls it wisdom. Christ names it as a casualty, and the verse immediately following is the promise to him that shall endure unto the end.

Revelation 3:15 makes the surprising preference explicit: I would thou wert cold or hot. Christ prefers either extreme to the lukewarm, which is the one condition He describes as nauseating. A cold church knows it is cold; a lukewarm one says I am rich, and increased with goods, and have need of nothing, and does not know that it is wretched, and miserable, and poor, and blind, and naked.
roots_summary: Hebrew qar (H7119), cold; qarah (H7135), coldness; Greek psuchros (G5593), cold — from psucho, to breathe out, to cool.
roots_lines: Greek psuchros (G5593) — cold; Matthew 10:42, Revelation 3:15-16.
Greek psucho (G5594) — to grow cool; only Matthew 24:12, shall wax cold.
Hebrew qar (H7119) — cold; Proverbs 25:25, Jeremiah 18:14.
usage: “Because iniquity shall abound, the love of many shall wax cold” — a mechanism, not a mood.
“I would thou wert cold or hot” — either extreme preferred to lukewarm.
“A cup of cold water only” — the smallest measurable kindness, rewarded.

pos: v. (to entrust; also to praise; rendering Greek paratithemi and sunistemi)
etymology: From Latin commendare, to entrust. The older sense is to hand over for safekeeping, which is how Christ uses it from the cross.
biblical_def: To commend is to entrust or to praise. Christ's last words use the first sense: “Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit” (Luk 23:46). Paul does the same for a church: “I commend you to God, and to the word of his grace, which is able to build you up” (Act 20:32). The second sense appears in the gospel's most compressed sentence: “God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us” (Rom 5:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines commend as to represent as worthy of notice, regard, or kindness; to speak in favor of; to recommend; to commit, to entrust or give in charge; and to praise, to mention with approbation.
webster_full: COMMEND, v.t. To represent as worthy of notice, regard, or kindness; to speak in favor of; to recommend.
2. To commit; to entrust or give in charge.
3. To praise; to mention with approbation.
4. To make acceptable or agreeable.
scriptures: And when Jesus had cried with a loud voice, he said, Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit: and having said thus, he gave up the ghost.
And now, brethren, I commend you to God, and to the word of his grace, which is able to build you up, and to give you an inheritance among all them which are sanctified.
Rom 5:8
But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.
For not he that commendeth himself is approved, but whom the Lord commendeth.
corruption_summary: Leaving people is treated as abandonment or as a failure of care, and Paul's farewell commends a church to God and the word rather than to a successor.
corruption_paragraphs: Acts 20:32 is one of the most instructive sentences ever spoken by a departing leader: and now, brethren, I commend you to God, and to the word of his grace, which is able to build you up, and to give you an inheritance among all them which are sanctified. He does not commend them to a man, a structure, or his own continuing oversight. Two things are named as sufficient, and the verb able attaches to the word rather than to Paul.

Romans 5:8 uses the other sense and compresses the gospel into a clause: God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us. Love is not asserted but demonstrated, and the timing is the proof — while we were yet sinners, not after any improvement. The word commendeth is present tense: the demonstration keeps standing.
roots_summary: Greek paratithemi (G3908), to place beside, entrust; sunistemi (G4921), to commend, prove; paratithemai is the verb of a deposit left with a trustee.
roots_lines: Greek paratithemi (G3908) — to entrust, commend; Luke 23:46, Acts 14:23, 20:32, 1 Peter 4:19.
Greek sunistemi (G4921) — to commend, demonstrate; Romans 5:8, 2 Corinthians 10:18.
Greek epainos (G1868) — praise; the other sense's noun.
usage: “Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit” — a deposit entrusted.
“I commend you to God, and to the word of his grace” — two things named sufficient.
“While we were yet sinners, Christ died for us” — love demonstrated, not asserted.

etymology: From Latin compellere, to drive together. The Greek aggareuo is a Persian loanword for a courier's right to press a civilian into carrying his load.
biblical_def: To compel is to force. Christ addresses the occupier's legal right directly: “whosoever shall compel thee to go a mile, go with him twain” (Mat 5:41). The same verb describes Simon of Cyrene, whom the soldiers “compelled to bear his cross” (Mat 27:32; Mar 15:21). The householder in the parable says, “Go out into the highways and hedges, and compel them to come in, that my house may be filled” (Luk 14:23), and Paul rebukes Peter for compelling Gentiles to live as Jews (Gal 2:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines compel as to drive or urge with force, or irresistibly; to constrain; to oblige; to necessitate, either by physical or moral force.
webster_full: COMPEL, v.t. To drive or urge with force, or irresistibly; to constrain; to oblige; to necessitate, either by physical or moral force.
2. To force; to take by force, or violence; to seize.
3. To drive together; to gather; to unite in a crowd or company.
scriptures: Mat 5:41
And whosoever shall compel thee to go a mile, go with him twain.
And as they came out, they found a man of Cyrene, Simon by name: him they compelled to bear his cross.
And the lord said unto the servant, Go out into the highways and hedges, and compel them to come in, that my house may be filled.
Gal 2:14

But when I saw that they walked not uprightly according to the truth of the gospel, I said unto Peter before them all, If thou, being a Jew, livest after the manner of Gentiles, and not as do the Jews, why compellest thou the Gentiles to live as do the Jews?
corruption_summary: Compulsion is resented as the end of freedom, and Christ's answer to a legally compelled mile is a second mile nobody could demand.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew 5:41 addresses a specific legal indignity. A Roman soldier could require any provincial to carry his pack one mile, and no further. Christ's instruction — go with him twain — concedes the compelled mile and then adds one that cannot be compelled. The first mile belongs to Rome; the second belongs to the disciple, and it is the only mile in the transaction that is free. Resentment cannot survive the second mile, which may be the point.

Luke 14:23 uses the same verb for the gospel invitation and has been badly misused: compel them to come in. The context is a master whose invited guests declined and whose servant reports there is yet room. The compelling is the urgency of an invitation pressed on people who cannot believe it is meant for them — the poor, the maimed, the halt, the blind — not a warrant for force, which the parable's own generosity forbids.
roots_summary: Greek aggareuo (G29), to press into public service — a Persian postal term; anagkazo (G315), to necessitate, constrain.
roots_lines: Greek aggareuo (G29) — to compel into service; Matthew 5:41, 27:32, Mark 15:21.
Greek anagkazo (G315) — to compel, constrain; Luke 14:23, Galatians 2:14, 2 Corinthians 12:11.
Greek milion (G3400) — a Roman mile; only Matthew 5:41.
usage: “Compel thee to go a mile, go with him twain” — the second mile is the free one.
“Him they compelled to bear his cross” — Simon of Cyrene, pressed into service.
“Compel them to come in, that my house may be filled” — urgency, not force.

etymology: From Latin concelare, to hide completely. Scripture distinguishes concealment that is glory from concealment that is treachery.
biblical_def: To conceal is to hide. Proverbs draws a striking distinction: “It is the glory of God to conceal a thing: but the honour of kings is to search out a matter” (Pro 25:2). It condemns the concealment that betrays: “A talebearer revealeth secrets: but he that is of a faithful spirit concealeth the matter” (Pro 11:13). The psalmist testifies, “I have not concealed thy lovingkindness and thy truth from the great congregation” (Psa 40:10), and Job says, “I have not concealed the words of the Holy One” (Job 6:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines conceal as to keep close or secret; to forbear to disclose; to withhold from utterance or declaration; and to hide, to withdraw from observation.
webster_full: CONCEAL, v.t. To keep close or secret; to forbear to disclose; to withhold from utterance or declaration.
2. To hide; to withdraw from observation; to cover or keep from sight.
scriptures: Pro 25:2
It is the glory of God to conceal a thing: but the honour of kings is to search out a matter.
A talebearer revealeth secrets: but he that is of a faithful spirit concealeth the matter.
I have not hid thy righteousness within my heart; I have declared thy faithfulness and thy salvation: I have not concealed thy lovingkindness and thy truth from the great congregation.
Job 6:10
Then should I yet have comfort; yea, I would harden myself in sorrow: let him not spare; for I have not concealed the words of the Holy One.
corruption_summary: Transparency is treated as an absolute good, and Proverbs commends the faithful man who conceals a matter and condemns the talebearer who reveals it.
corruption_paragraphs: Proverbs 11:13 sets two men side by side: a talebearer revealeth secrets: but he that is of a faithful spirit concealeth the matter. Concealment here is a mark of faithfulness. A friend who repeats what he was told, however accurately, has failed a test that has nothing to do with honesty — the information was true and the telling was a betrayal. Discretion and deceit are not the same thing, and a culture that cannot tell them apart will destroy confidences in the name of openness.

Proverbs 25:2 sets the other boundary: it is the glory of God to conceal a thing: but the honour of kings is to search out a matter. God's hiddenness is His glory; a ruler's business is investigation. Both are honourable and they are not in conflict — which means a believer may hold both an unembarrassed acceptance of divine mystery and a rigorous curiosity about everything that can actually be found out.
roots_summary: Hebrew kachad (H3582), to hide, conceal; kasah (H3680), to cover; chaqar (H2713), to search out — the king's work in Proverbs 25:2.
roots_lines: Hebrew kachad (H3582) — to hide, conceal; Psalm 40:10, Job 6:10, 27:11.
Hebrew kasah (H3680) — to cover, conceal; Proverbs 11:13, 25:2, 28:13.
Hebrew chaqar (H2713) — to search out; Proverbs 25:2, the honour of kings.
usage: “It is the glory of God to conceal a thing” — hiddenness as glory.
“He that is of a faithful spirit concealeth the matter” — discretion as faithfulness.
“I have not concealed thy lovingkindness… from the great congregation” — the one thing not to hide.

etymology: From Latin contentus, held together, restrained. Contentment is a boundary held rather than a desire satisfied.
biblical_def: Content means satisfied. Paul states it as an acquired skill: “I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content” (Php 4:11), and specifies both directions — “I know both how to be abased, and I know how to abound” (Php 4:12). He gives the minimum: “having food and raiment let us be therewith content” (1Ti 6:8). Hebrews grounds it in a promise: “be content with such things as ye have: for he hath said, I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee” (Heb 13:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines content as literally, held, contained within limits; hence, quiet; not disturbed; having a mind at peace; easy; satisfied, so as not to repine, object, or oppose.
webster_full: CONTENT, a. Literally, held, contained within limits; hence, quiet; not disturbed; having a mind at peace; easy; satisfied, so as not to repine, object, or oppose.
scriptures: Php 4:11
Not that I speak in respect of want: for I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content.
Php 4:12
I know both how to be abased, and I know how to abound: every where and in all things I am instructed both to be full and to be hungry, both to abound and to suffer need.
And having food and raiment let us be therewith content.
Heb 13:5
Let your conversation be without covetousness; and be content with such things as ye have: for he hath said, I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee.
corruption_summary: Contentment is expected to arrive with sufficiency, and Paul calls it something learned — and reports learning it in abundance as well as in want.
corruption_paragraphs: Philippians 4:11-12 is written from prison and makes contentment a curriculum rather than a temperament: I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content. I know both how to be abased, and I know how to abound… both to be full and to be hungry, both to abound and to suffer need. Two directions are named, and abundance is listed as a condition requiring instruction. Most people assume only want needs a lesson.

Hebrews 13:5 supplies the reason that makes it possible: let your conversation be without covetousness; and be content with such things as ye have: for he hath said, I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee. The argument runs from a promise about Presence to a conclusion about possessions. Contentment is not talked into existence by lowering expectations; it follows from a settled fact about who is staying.
roots_summary: Greek autarkes (G842), self-sufficient, content; autarkeia (G841), contentment; arkeo (G714), to be enough.
roots_lines: Greek autarkes (G842) — content, self-sufficient; only Philippians 4:11.
Greek autarkeia (G841) — contentment; 1 Timothy 6:6, 2 Corinthians 9:8.
Greek arkeo (G714) — to suffice, be content; Hebrews 13:5, 1 Timothy 6:8.
usage: “I have learned… therewith to be content” — a curriculum, not a temperament.
“I know both how to be abased, and… how to abound” — abundance needed teaching too.
“Be content… for he hath said, I will never leave thee” — possessions answered by Presence.

etymology: From Latin convenire, to come together, to be fitting. In the KJV convenient means proper or suitable, not merely easy.
biblical_def: Convenient means fitting. Agur's prayer uses it of provision: “give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with food convenient for me” (Pro 30:8) — the portion suited to him. Paul uses it of speech: “neither filthiness, nor foolish talking, nor jesting, which are not convenient” (Eph 5:4). He appeals to Philemon on love's ground rather than authority, though he might “enjoin thee that which is convenient” (Phm 8). Felix defers Paul until a convenient season (Act 24:25).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines convenient as fit; suitable; proper; adapted to use or to wants; and commodious, well adapted to use.
webster_full: CONVENIENT, a. Fit; suitable; proper; adapted to use or to wants.
2. Commodious; well adapted to use.
3. Fit; adapted; suitable; becoming.
scriptures: Pro 30:8
Remove far from me vanity and lies: give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with food convenient for me:
Eph 5:4
Neither filthiness, nor foolish talking, nor jesting, which are not convenient: but rather giving of thanks.
Phm 8
Wherefore, though I might be much bold in Christ to enjoin thee that which is convenient,
And as he reasoned of righteousness, temperance, and judgment to come, Felix trembled, and answered, Go thy way for this time; when I have a convenient season, I will call for thee.
corruption_summary: Convenient has drifted to mean easy, and the KJV means fitting — which is why Agur asks for food convenient for him rather than for more.
corruption_paragraphs: Proverbs 30:8-9 is one of the few prayers in Scripture that asks God to withhold wealth, and it gives reasons for both requests: give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with food convenient for me: lest I be full, and deny thee, and say, Who is the LORD? or lest I be poor, and steal, and take the name of my God in vain. Agur knows both extremes carry a specific spiritual danger, and he asks for the portion fitted to him rather than the largest available.

Acts 24:25 shows the word's other, chilling use. Paul reasoned of righteousness, temperance, and judgment to come, Felix trembled, and answered, Go thy way for this time; when I have a convenient season, I will call for thee. The convenient season never came. A man moved enough to tremble deferred the matter to a better moment, and Scripture records no better moment arriving.
roots_summary: Hebrew choq (H2706), an allotted portion; Greek aneko (G433), to be fitting; eukairos (G2121), well-timed, convenient.
roots_lines: Hebrew choq (H2706) — portion, allotted thing; Proverbs 30:8, food convenient for me.
Greek aneko (G433) — to be fitting, convenient; Ephesians 5:4, Philemon 8, Colossians 3:18.
Greek eukairos (G2121) — convenient, opportune; Acts 24:25, Mark 6:21.
usage: “Feed me with food convenient for me” — the fitted portion, not the largest.
“Foolish talking, nor jesting, which are not convenient” — speech judged by fitness.
“When I have a convenient season” — a season that never came.

etymology: From Latin corrumpere, to break utterly. Corruptible names what is capable of decaying, which in Scripture is nearly everything visible.
biblical_def: Corruptible means subject to decay. Peter uses it to price redemption: “ye were not redeemed with corruptible things, as silver and gold… but with the precious blood of Christ” (1Pe 1:18–19). Paul contrasts crowns: athletes strive “to obtain a corruptible crown; but we an incorruptible” (1Co 9:25). The resurrection reverses it: “this corruptible must put on incorruption” (1Co 15:53), and idolatry is described as changing the glory of the uncorruptible God into an image like corruptible man (Rom 1:23).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines corruptible as that may be corrupted; that may be vitiated or depraved; and subject to decay and destruction.
webster_full: CORRUPTIBLE, a. That may be corrupted; that may be vitiated or depraved in morals.
2. That may be corrupted, or rotted; subject to decay and destruction.
scriptures: Forasmuch as ye know that ye were not redeemed with corruptible things, as silver and gold, from your vain conversation received by tradition from your fathers;
And every man that striveth for the mastery is temperate in all things. Now they do it to obtain a corruptible crown; but we an incorruptible.
For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality.
Rom 1:23
And changed the glory of the uncorruptible God into an image made like to corruptible man, and to birds, and fourfooted beasts, and creeping things.
corruption_summary: Money is the standard of value, and Peter files silver and gold under corruptible things before naming what actually purchased anyone.
corruption_paragraphs: 1 Peter 1:18 makes a valuation that no market would accept: forasmuch as ye know that ye were not redeemed with corruptible things, as silver and gold, from your vain conversation received by tradition from your fathers; but with the precious blood of Christ. The metals every economy is built on are classed with everything else that rots. The price of a soul was not merely higher than silver; it was of a different order of substance.

1 Corinthians 15:53 states the resurrection's mechanism in one clause: this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality. The word this is doing important work — the same body, not a replacement. Paul is not describing an escape from the material but its clothing in something that cannot decay, which is why he ends the chapter with a command about steadfast labour rather than about waiting.
roots_lines: Greek phthartos (G5349) — corruptible; 1 Peter 1:18, 23, 1 Corinthians 9:25, 15:53-54, Romans 1:23.
Greek aphthartos (G862) — incorruptible; 1 Peter 1:4, 1 Corinthians 9:25.
Greek enduo (G1746) — to put on; 1 Corinthians 15:53, must put on incorruption.
usage: “Not redeemed with corruptible things, as silver and gold” — the metals filed under rot.
“They do it to obtain a corruptible crown; but we an incorruptible” — two prizes compared.
“This corruptible must put on incorruption” — the same body, newly clothed.

pos: adj. (of great price; rendering Greek polutimos and poluteles)
etymology: From cost, Latin constare, to stand at a price. Costly in Scripture usually marks either a lavish devotion or an inappropriate display.
biblical_def: Costly means of great price. Mary anoints Christ with “a pound of ointment of spikenard, very costly”, and the house was filled with the odour (Joh 12:3). Solomon's temple used costly stones (1Ki 7:9–11). Peter directs women's adorning away from “costly array” toward a meek and quiet spirit (1Pe 3:3–4), and Paul gives the same instruction to Timothy's church (1Ti 2:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines costly as of a high price; sumptuous; expensive; purchased at a great expense.
webster_full: COSTLY, a. Of a high price; sumptuous; expensive; purchased at a great expense; as a costly habit; costly furniture.
scriptures: Joh 12:3
Then took Mary a pound of ointment of spikenard, very costly, and anointed the feet of Jesus, and wiped his feet with her hair: and the house was filled with the odour of the ointment.
Whose adorning let it not be that outward adorning of plaiting the hair, and of wearing of gold, or of putting on of apparel;
In like manner also, that women adorn themselves in modest apparel, with shamefacedness and sobriety; not with broided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly array;

All these were of costly stones, according to the measures of hewed stones, sawed with saws, within and without, even from the foundation unto the coping, and so on the outside toward the great court.
corruption_summary: Costliness is judged by the amount rather than the direction, and Scripture commends a year's wages poured on Christ's feet while restraining costly array on oneself.
corruption_paragraphs: The two uses are not in tension once the direction is noticed. Mary's ointment was very costly and is defended by Christ against every objection — let her alone: against the day of my burying hath she kept this. Peter and Paul restrain costly array, which is expenditure aimed at the wearer's own display. The same money is commended poured out and questioned worn.

1 Peter 3:4 supplies the substitute rather than merely a prohibition: but let it be the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price. The phrase of great price is the same valuation language — Peter does not tell women to want nothing costly; he tells them where the genuinely expensive item is.
roots_summary: Greek polutimos (G4186), of great price; poluteles (G4185), very costly — used of both the ointment and the meek spirit.
roots_lines: Greek polutimos (G4186) — very costly, precious; John 12:3, Matthew 13:46, 1 Peter 1:7.
Greek poluteles (G4185) — very costly; Mark 14:3, 1 Timothy 2:9, 1 Peter 3:4.
Greek nardos pistike — pure spikenard; John 12:3, the imported ointment.
usage: “Ointment of spikenard, very costly” — poured out and defended.
“Not with broided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly array” — expenditure aimed inward.
“In the sight of God of great price” — where the expensive item actually is.

pos: n. (the One who creates; rendering Hebrew bore, Greek ktistes)
etymology: From Latin creare, to bring forth. The Hebrew bara is used in Scripture only with God as its subject — no creature ever creates.
biblical_def: The Creator is God as maker. Ecclesiastes closes its argument with Him: “Remember now thy Creator in the days of thy youth, while the evil days come not” (Ecc 12:1). Isaiah asks, “Hast thou not known? hast thou not heard, that the everlasting God, the LORD, the Creator of the ends of the earth, fainteth not, neither is weary?” (Isa 40:28). Romans names the fundamental exchange: they “worshipped and served the creature more than the Creator, who is blessed for ever” (Rom 1:25). Peter commends souls to Him as “a faithful Creator” (1Pe 4:19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines creator as the being or person that creates; and by way of eminence, the Supreme Being, the author of existence.
webster_full: CREATOR, n. The being or person that creates.
2. By way of eminence, the Supreme Being, the author of existence.
scriptures: Ecc 12:1
Remember now thy Creator in the days of thy youth, while the evil days come not, nor the years draw nigh, when thou shalt say, I have no pleasure in them;
Hast thou not known? hast thou not heard, that the everlasting God, the LORD, the Creator of the ends of the earth, fainteth not, neither is weary? there is no searching of his understanding.
Rom 1:25
Who changed the truth of God into a lie, and worshipped and served the creature more than the Creator, who is blessed for ever. Amen.
Wherefore let them that suffer according to the will of God commit the keeping of their souls to him in well doing, as unto a faithful Creator.
corruption_summary: Creation is discussed as a question about origins, and Scripture treats the Creator as a Person to be remembered, trusted, and worshipped rather than a theory to be held.
corruption_paragraphs: Ecclesiastes 12:1 does not argue for a Creator; it commands remembering one: remember now thy Creator in the days of thy youth, while the evil days come not, nor the years draw nigh, when thou shalt say, I have no pleasure in them. The book has spent eleven chapters demonstrating that everything under the sun is vapour, and its single positive instruction is a relationship with the Maker, entered early.

1 Peter 4:19 gives the title its most practical use: wherefore let them that suffer according to the will of God commit the keeping of their souls to him in well doing, as unto a faithful Creator. Peter chooses Creator rather than Redeemer or Father for suffering Christians, and adds faithful. The One who made a soul can be trusted with keeping it, and the argument runs from workmanship to reliability.
roots_summary: Hebrew bore (H1254), Creator — participle of bara, a verb whose subject in Scripture is always God; Greek ktistes (G2939), creator.
roots_lines: Hebrew bara (H1254) — to create; Genesis 1:1, Isaiah 40:28, Ecclesiastes 12:1.
Greek ktistes (G2939) — creator; only 1 Peter 4:19.
Greek ktisis (G2937) — creation, creature; Romans 1:25, the creature more than the Creator.
usage: “Remember now thy Creator in the days of thy youth” — the book's one positive instruction.
“The Creator of the ends of the earth, fainteth not” — offered to the weary.
“As unto a faithful Creator” — the title chosen for sufferers.

pos: adj. (bent, not straight; rendering Hebrew iqqesh, Greek skolios)
etymology: From crook, a bend. Crookedness in Scripture is moral before it is geometric, and only God is said to be able to straighten it.
biblical_def: Crooked means bent. Ecclesiastes states a limit: “That which is crooked cannot be made straight: and that which is wanting cannot be numbered” (Ecc 1:15), and elsewhere asks who can make that straight which God hath made crooked (Ecc 7:13). Isaiah promises the opposite as gospel: “the crooked shall be made straight, and the rough places plain” (Isa 40:4), quoted of John the Baptist (Luk 3:5). Paul tells the Philippians to shine as lights “in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation” (Php 2:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines crooked as bending; curved; not straight; and figuratively, perverse; untoward; deviating from rectitude.
webster_full: CROOKED, a. Bending; curving; winding; not straight.
2. Perverse; untoward; deviating from rectitude or moral rectitude; froward.
3. Winding in moral conduct; devious; not upright.
scriptures: Ecc 1:15
That which is crooked cannot be made straight: and that which is wanting cannot be numbered.
Isa 40:4
Every valley shall be exalted, and every mountain and hill shall be made low: and the crooked shall be made straight, and the rough places plain:
Luk 3:5
Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be brought low; and the crooked shall be made straight, and the rough ways shall be made smooth;
Php 2:15
That ye may be blameless and harmless, the sons of God, without rebuke, in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, among whom ye shine as lights in the world;
corruption_summary: Self-improvement is assumed capable of straightening anything, and Ecclesiastes states flatly that what is crooked cannot be made straight — by us.
corruption_paragraphs: Ecclesiastes 1:15 is one of the Preacher's bleakest observations and it is entirely accurate within its frame: that which is crooked cannot be made straight: and that which is wanting cannot be numbered. Under the sun, nobody unbends what is bent. Isaiah 40:4 answers it from outside that frame — the crooked shall be made straight — and the answer is announced by a voice preparing the way of the LORD. The two verses are not in conflict; they name what man cannot do and what God will.

Philippians 2:15 places the believer inside the crookedness rather than out of it: that ye may be blameless and harmless, the sons of God, without rebuke, in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, among whom ye shine as lights in the world. The straightness is not achieved by relocating. It is exhibited in place, and the verse before it names what makes that possible: do all things without murmurings and disputings.
roots_summary: Hebrew iqqesh (H6141), crooked, perverse; avath (H5791), to bend; Greek skolios (G4646), crooked — the same word as untoward in Acts 2:40.
roots_lines: Hebrew avath (H5791) — to bend, make crooked; Ecclesiastes 1:15, 7:13.
Hebrew iqqesh (H6141) — crooked, perverse; Deuteronomy 32:5, Proverbs 2:15.
Greek skolios (G4646) — crooked; Luke 3:5, Philippians 2:15, Acts 2:40.
usage: “That which is crooked cannot be made straight” — true under the sun.
“The crooked shall be made straight” — answered from outside that frame.
“In the midst of a crooked and perverse nation… ye shine” — straightness exhibited in place.

pos: v. (to press or break by weight; rendering Hebrew daka and ratsats)
etymology: From Old French croissir, to break. Crushing in Scripture is what the powerful do to the poor, and what God will not do to the bruised.
biblical_def: To crush is to break by pressure. Lamentations denies it of God's disposition: “to crush under his feet all the prisoners of the earth… the Lord approveth not” (Lam 3:34–36). Amos addresses the women of Samaria as those “which oppress the poor, which crush the needy” (Amo 4:1). Balaam's ass crushes his foot against a wall (Num 22:25), and Job's friend says his children are “crushed in the gate, neither is there any to deliver them” (Job 5:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines crush as to press and bruise between two hard bodies; to squeeze, so as to force a thing out of its natural shape; to break, to bruise; and to overwhelm by pressure.
webster_full: CRUSH, v.t. To press and bruise between two hard bodies; to squeeze, so as to force a thing out of its natural shape.
2. To press with violence; to force together into a mass.
3. To overwhelm by pressure; to beat or force down, by an incumbent weight, with breaking or bruising.
4. To oppress grievously.
scriptures: Lam 3:34
To crush under his feet all the prisoners of the earth,
Lam 3:36
To subvert a man in his cause, the Lord approveth not.
Amo 4:1
Hear this word, ye kine of Bashan, that are in the mountain of Samaria, which oppress the poor, which crush the needy, which say to their masters, Bring, and let us drink.
Job 5:4
His children are far from safety, and they are crushed in the gate, neither is there any to deliver them.
corruption_summary: Economic pressure on the poor is discussed in abstractions, and Amos addresses it in the second person to comfortable women at dinner.
corruption_paragraphs: Amos 4:1 is startlingly direct: hear this word, ye kine of Bashan, that are in the mountain of Samaria, which oppress the poor, which crush the needy, which say to their masters, Bring, and let us drink. The crushing is not done by policy or by markets in the abstract; it is done by particular comfortable people asking for another drink. Amos names the mechanism as an order given at a table, which is where most oppression is actually transacted.

Lamentations 3:34-36 sets the boundary: to crush under his feet all the prisoners of the earth, to turn aside the right of a man… the Lord approveth not. The passage sits in the middle of the book's darkest chapter, two verses after his compassions fail not. Even while Jerusalem lies in ruins by God's own judgment, the writer insists God does not approve the crushing of prisoners — which distinguishes judgment from cruelty.
roots_summary: Hebrew daka (H1792), to crush — the verb of Isaiah 53:10; ratsats (H7533), to break in pieces — the bruised reed of Isaiah 42:3.
roots_lines: Hebrew daka (H1792) — to crush, bruise; Lamentations 3:34, Isaiah 53:5, 10.
Hebrew ratsats (H7533) — to crush, oppress; Amos 4:1, Isaiah 42:3, a bruised reed shall he not break.
Hebrew dakka (H1793) — contrite, crushed; Isaiah 57:15, with him that is of a contrite heart.
usage: “Which oppress the poor, which crush the needy” — addressed in the second person.
“The Lord approveth not” — a boundary drawn inside the judgment.
“A bruised reed shall he not break” — the same root, denied of the Messiah.

pos: n., adj. (selection; also the best; rendering Hebrew mibchar, Greek eklogē)
etymology: From Old French chois. In the KJV choice most often means the best of a kind rather than the act of choosing.
biblical_def: Choice means selection, and as an adjective, the best. The Hittites offer Abraham “the choice of our sepulchres” for Sarah (Gen 23:6). Wisdom says, “Receive my instruction, and not silver; and knowledge rather than choice gold” (Pro 8:10). Peter tells the council that God “made choice among us, that the Gentiles by my mouth should hear the word of the gospel” (Act 15:7), and Joshua sets the famous alternative: “choose you this day whom ye will serve” (Jos 24:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines choice as the act of choosing; the voluntary act of selecting or separating from two or more things that which is preferred; and the best part, that which is preferable.
webster_full: CHOICE, n. The act of choosing; the voluntary act of selecting or separating from two or more things that which is preferred.
2. The power of choosing; option.
3. Care in selecting; judgment or skill in distinguishing what is to be preferred.
4. The thing chosen; that which is approved and selected in preference to others.
CHOICE, a. Worthy of being preferred; select; precious; very valuable.
scriptures: And if it seem evil unto you to serve the LORD, choose you this day whom ye will serve; whether the gods which your fathers served that were on the other side of the flood, or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land ye dwell: but as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.
Pro 8:10
Receive my instruction, and not silver; and knowledge rather than choice gold.
Act 15:7

And when there had been much disputing, Peter rose up, and said unto them, Men and brethren, ye know how that a good while ago God made choice among us, that the Gentiles by my mouth should hear the word of the gospel, and believe.
Gen 23:6
Hear us, my lord: thou art a mighty prince among us: in the choice of our sepulchres bury thy dead; none of us shall withhold from thee his sepulchre, but that thou mayest bury thy dead. a
corruption_summary: Choice is treated as the highest good in itself, and Joshua's famous verse assumes the only real question is which master, not whether to serve one.
corruption_paragraphs: Joshua 24:15 is quoted for its second half and its first half is the argument: and if it seem evil unto you to serve the LORD, choose you this day whom ye will serve; whether the gods which your fathers served… or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land ye dwell: but as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD. Service is assumed; only the object is open. Joshua offers no third option of serving nothing, because he does not think one exists.

The adjectival sense governs Proverbs 8:10 and sharpens the comparison: receive my instruction, and not silver; and knowledge rather than choice gold. Not gold, but choice gold — the best available specimen of the most valuable metal. Wisdom is not being compared with a poor alternative but with the finest one, which is the only comparison worth making.
roots_summary: Hebrew mibchar (H4005), choicest, best; bachar (H977), to choose; Greek eklogē (G1589), a selection.
roots_lines: Hebrew bachar (H977) — to choose; Joshua 24:15, 22, Deuteronomy 30:19, choose life.
Hebrew mibchar (H4005) — choicest, best; Genesis 23:6, Isaiah 22:7.
Greek eklogē (G1589) — choice, election; Acts 9:15, Romans 9:11, 11:5.
usage: “Choose you this day whom ye will serve” — service assumed, object open.
“Knowledge rather than choice gold” — compared with the finest specimen.
“God made choice among us” — Peter on the Gentile mission.

pos: adv. (according to the flesh; rendering Greek sarx)
etymology: From Latin caro, flesh. Carnal in Paul does not mean bodily but flesh-governed — a mind set on what the fallen nature wants.
biblical_def: Carnally means according to the flesh. Paul states the alternative starkly: “For to be carnally minded is death; but to be spiritually minded is life and peace” (Rom 8:6), and gives the reason: “because the carnal mind is enmity against God: for it is not subject to the law of God, neither indeed can be” (Rom 8:7). He rebukes the Corinthians as carnal because of envying, strife, and divisions (1Co 3:3), and Leviticus uses the word literally of unlawful union (Lev 18:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines carnal as pertaining to flesh; fleshly; sensual; opposed to spiritual; and being in the natural state, unregenerate.
webster_full: CARNAL, a. Pertaining to flesh; fleshly; sensual; opposed to spiritual.
2. Being in the natural state; unregenerate.
3. Pertaining to the ceremonial law; as carnal ordinances.
CARNALLY, adv. In a carnal manner; according to the flesh.
scriptures: Rom 8:6
For to be carnally minded is death; but to be spiritually minded is life and peace.
Rom 8:7
Because the carnal mind is enmity against God: for it is not subject to the law of God, neither indeed can be.
For ye are yet carnal: for whereas there is among you envying, and strife, and divisions, are ye not carnal, and walk as men?
Rom 8:8
So then they that are in the flesh cannot please God.
corruption_summary: Carnality is imagined as gross indulgence, and Paul's example is a church quarrelling over which preacher it prefers.
corruption_paragraphs: 1 Corinthians 3:3 supplies the evidence Paul accepts for the charge: for ye are yet carnal: for whereas there is among you envying, and strife, and divisions, are ye not carnal, and walk as men? The symptoms are not scandals but factions — I am of Paul; and I of Apollos. Church division is diagnosed as flesh, which means a congregation can be doctrinally careful, morally respectable, and carnal at the same time.

Romans 8:7 states why the condition cannot be improved from within: because the carnal mind is enmity against God: for it is not subject to the law of God, neither indeed can be. Not merely unwilling — unable. That closes the door on reform as a remedy and requires something else entirely, which is why the chapter opens with no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus and proceeds to the Spirit of life.
roots_summary: Greek sarx (G4561), flesh; sarkikos (G4559), fleshly, carnal; phronema tes sarkos, the mind of the flesh, in Romans 8:6.
roots_lines: Greek sarkikos (G4559) — carnal, fleshly; 1 Corinthians 3:1-4, Romans 15:27.
Greek phronema (G5427) — mind, mindset; Romans 8:6-7, the carnal mind.
Greek pneumatikos (G4152) — spiritual; the contrasting term throughout.
usage: “To be carnally minded is death” — the alternative stated starkly.
“Envying, and strife, and divisions… are ye not carnal?” — factions as evidence.
“Neither indeed can be” — why reform is not the remedy.
